title: Shortcode delimiter not separated by a space
message: A shortcode's delimiters must be separated from its content by whitespace. Write `{{< fa plus >}}` — a space after `{{<` and a space before `>}}` — rather than `{{<fa plus>}}`.
hints: Both delimiters need the space. Adding it to only one of them leaves the shortcode unparseable.

Quarto 1 accepted the tight spelling because it matched shortcodes with a regular expression. Quarto 2 parses them, and requires the space so that `{{` stays unambiguous with template syntaxes such as Jinja and Handlebars.
`qmd-syntax-helper convert -r q-2-52 -i <file>` rewrites both delimiters for you.

cases.name: opening-delimiter
cases.description: No space after `{{<`. This is the spelling Quarto 1 projects arrive with; the Positron docs had seven occurrences in one file.

cases.name: opening-delimiter-in-inline-container
cases.description: The opening delimiter is consumed in the *enclosing* inline container's parser state, so unlike the closing delimiter it needs a case per container. Each prefix/suffix pair below reaches a distinct LR state; the four editorial spellings share one, and link text, image alt text and bracketed span text share another.

cases.name: opening-delimiter-in-table-header-cell
cases.description: Pipe-table cells are built on `_line_with_maybe_spaces`, a sibling of the `_inlines` every other inline container wraps, so they reach their own states — one for header cells, one for body cells.

cases.name: opening-delimiter-in-table-body-cell
cases.description: The body-cell state, distinct from the header-cell state above.

cases.name: escaped-opening-delimiter
cases.description: The escaped spelling `{{{< ... >}}}` takes the separator too, and its opening delimiter reaches its own state. Its *closing* delimiter needs no case of its own: by then the parser is inside the shortcode, in the same state the unescaped form reaches, and the guard matches `>}}}` as readily as `>}}`.

cases.name: escaped-opening-delimiter-in-inline-container
cases.description: One state per enclosing inline container, as for the unescaped opening delimiter.

cases.name: escaped-opening-delimiter-in-table-header-cell
cases.description: Pipe-table header cell.

cases.name: escaped-opening-delimiter-in-table-body-cell
cases.description: Pipe-table body cell, a distinct state from the header cell.

cases.name: closing-delimiter-after-name-only
cases.description: A shortcode with no arguments. Unlike every other closing-delimiter spelling, this one is container-dependent: with nothing after the name the parser has not committed to the shortcode's argument list, so the state still follows the enclosing inline container.

cases.name: closing-delimiter-after-name-only-in-inline-container
cases.description: The container family of the case above.

cases.name: escaped-closing-delimiter-after-name-only
cases.description: The escaped spelling of the no-argument form; its own state family again.

cases.name: escaped-closing-delimiter-after-name-only-in-inline-container
cases.description: The container family of the case above.

cases.name: closing-delimiter-after-non-language-specifier-value
cases.description: An unquoted argument that the external `_language_specifier_token` scanner does not claim — anything not starting with an ASCII letter or digit, and anything non-ASCII — is produced by the `shortcode_naked_string` regex instead, and reaches its own state. `{{< fa größe>}}`, `{{< fa /path/x>}}` and `{{< fa k=größe>}}` all land here.

cases.name: closing-delimiter-after-name-only-in-table-header-cell
cases.description: The no-argument closing delimiter is container-dependent, and pipe-table cells are not reachable by wrapping a line in a prefix and suffix, so the two cell states need cases of their own.

cases.name: closing-delimiter-after-name-only-in-table-body-cell
cases.description: The body-cell state, distinct from the header-cell state above.

cases.name: escaped-closing-delimiter-after-name-only-in-table-header-cell
cases.description: The escaped spelling in a header cell.

cases.name: escaped-closing-delimiter-after-name-only-in-table-body-cell
cases.description: The escaped spelling in a body cell.

cases.name: closing-delimiter-after-single-quoted-value
cases.description: A single-quoted argument. The scanner has a separate token for single-character quoted content, so `'q'` and `'quoted'` reach different states and both need a case.

cases.name: closing-delimiter-after-one-character-single-quoted-value
cases.description: The single-character spelling of the case above.

cases.name: closing-delimiter-after-one-character-double-quoted-value
cases.description: The single-character spelling of `closing-delimiter-after-quoted-value`.

cases.name: closing-delimiter-after-nested-shortcode
cases.description: A shortcode used as another shortcode's argument. The escaped outer spelling (`{{{< fa {{< b >}}>}}}`) reaches this same state. An *escaped* shortcode cannot be an argument at all — `_shortcode_value` admits `shortcode`, not `shortcode_escaped` — so `{{{< fa {{{< b >}}} >}}}` fails whether or not the space is there, and is deliberately not claimed here.

cases.name: escaped-closing-delimiter-after-keyword-value
cases.description: An escaped shortcode ending in a keyword argument. The unescaped spelling shares its state with the positional form; the escaped one does not, and it blames the argument's value rather than the delimiter. That state is shared with Q-2-28 (a line break before `>}}}`), so this case is guarded on the delimiter following the value with no whitespace between — which is exactly what distinguishes the two.

cases.name: nested-shortcode-opening-delimiter
cases.description: A shortcode used as another shortcode's argument has its own state for the inner opening delimiter. Container-independent, and shared with the escaped outer spelling. Once the inner shortcode has an argument of its own the closing delimiter collapses to `closing-delimiter`'s state.

cases.name: nested-shortcode-closing-delimiter
cases.description: The inner closing delimiter of a nested shortcode.

cases.name: opening-delimiter-in-double-quoted-attribute-value
cases.description: A shortcode inside an attribute value. The quoting style changes the state, so both spellings need a case.

cases.name: opening-delimiter-in-single-quoted-attribute-value
cases.description: The single-quoted spelling of the case above.

cases.name: closing-delimiter-in-attribute-value
cases.description: The closing delimiter inside an attribute value, before the shortcode takes any argument.

cases.name: opening-delimiter-in-link-destination
cases.description: A shortcode used to build a link or image destination. One state covers links, images and destinations where the shortcode is only part of the path.

cases.name: closing-delimiter-in-link-destination
cases.description: The closing delimiter inside a link destination, before the shortcode takes any argument.

cases.name: closing-delimiter
cases.description: No space before `>}}`, after an unquoted argument. This state is shared with Q-2-34 (an unquoted value that starts with a digit), which fails on the same lookahead in the same state, so this case is guarded: it claims the state only when the error is *at* the closing delimiter. `{{< fa 2plus>}}` has both faults and stays with Q-2-34, which is the earlier and more specific of the two. Unlike the opening delimiter, the parser is already inside the shortcode here, so one case covers every inline container.

cases.name: closing-delimiter-after-quoted-value
cases.description: No space before `>}}`, after a quoted argument. A different state from the unquoted form — and the spelling an author reaches for when Q-2-34 tells them to quote the value.
